headline: Slow-grinding world: frontier defaults, a bond scare in Tokyo, and AI gains for the few

events: US extends sectoral tariffs to pharma inputs and legacy chips; EU answers with targeted steel and EV safeguards rather than full retaliation
Ukraine front freezes into an unratified ceasefire line; European defence budgets rise toward 2.5-3% of GDP, financed mostly by borrowing
Fed trims to 3.25% then pauses as core inflation sticks near 3%; ECB at 2%
AI capex keeps climbing but enterprise adoption reaches only ~16% of firms; back-office hiring freezes spread in banking and insurance
Two frontier economies in Africa seek Common Framework restructuring after Eurobond rollovers fail
Wildcard: a weak 30-year JGB auction triggers a disorderly yen and yield spike; BoJ reinstates a soft yield cap and halts balance-sheet run-off
US election campaign dominated by housing costs and AI layoffs; winner promises more tariffs and a 'reshoring tax credit' adding ~0.5% of GDP to deficits
Global growth dips to 2.2% as China's exports to the West slow and its local-government debt swaps crowd out investment
Oil spikes briefly to $105 on a Gulf shipping incident, pushing G20 average inflation to a ~4% peak
Pakistan and a Latin American sovereign negotiate emergency IMF programmes
AI-capex correction: hyperscalers cut 2030 guidance by a fifth, tech equities fall ~30%, data-centre power contracts renegotiated
Global unemployment peaks at ~5.6% as the slowdown hits construction and white-collar services together
Sahel-to-coastal West Africa conflict escalates into a cross-border war drawing in regional states and foreign mercenaries
China launches a large but quiet consumption-support package and expands yuan trade settlement with Gulf and ASEAN partners
COP34 produces a methane deal but no tightening of 2035 targets
Recovery to ~2.7% growth; cheaper inference and agentic tools push AI use to ~24% of firms, mostly in large companies
US debt passes 130% of GDP; interest costs exceed defence spending; a bond-market wobble forces a modest bipartisan spending cap
Record heatwave in South Asia and a failed monsoon push food inflation in India and Bangladesh; rice export bans return
EU agrees a second joint borrowing round for defence and grid investment, a small step toward fiscal union
Renewables pass 40% of global electricity as Chinese solar overcapacity floods Global South markets
Growth settles near 2.8%; inflation ~3% and policy rates ~3.25% globally, a 'higher-for-ever' equilibrium
A fourth sovereign default (a Middle-Eastern import-dependent state) is handled through a slow, partial restructuring
Trade blocs harden around technology standards: separate AI chip, cloud and payment ecosystems in US-aligned and China-aligned spheres
Youth unemployment protests in several African and Latin American cities; populist parties in government in a third of the EU
Global temperature anomaly averages ~1.6C; 1.5C is officially acknowledged as overshot

winners: Large AI and cloud platform firms with cheap capital and energy contracts
Gulf states and India as bloc-swing 'connector' economies
losers: Indebted frontier economies in Africa and South Asia shut out of markets
Young renters and junior white-collar workers in advanced economies
Japanese savers and fixed-income pensioners hit by the JGB scare and inflation
bullets: The world never crashed, but it grew roughly half a point slower each year than the 2010s, and nobody had the fiscal room to change that.
Public debt crept past 100% of world GDP; interest bills now crowd out climate, aid and education spending almost everywhere.
Trade is organised into two loose blocs with a busy middle of connector states; tariffs are higher, but goods still flow through rerouted supply chains.
AI is used by under a third of firms; productivity gains are real but concentrated in large firms, while entry-level office jobs have quietly thinned out.
Four sovereign defaults and a long West African war have reversed development gains across parts of Africa, deepening migration pressure on Europe.
Renewables are above 40% of electricity thanks to cheap Chinese hardware, but emissions have only plateaued and warming hit about 1.6C.
Trust in institutions has eroded further; politics is volatile, with incumbents ousted often but policy changing little.
Central banks remain the most credible actors, holding inflation near 3% and quietly tolerating financial repression of savers.
wildcard: A failed 30-year Japanese government bond auction in 2028 forced the Bank of Japan to reinstate yield control amid a yen panic.
image_description: In a cramped Madrid flat in 2031, three thirtysomething flatmates eat cheap takeaway under a heat-alert banner on their wall screen while an AI agent negotiates their next rent increase and the news ticker scrolls tariff updates.
